transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Radei.
I'm your host, Eddie Pungen, and today we're delighted to have Ryan Bunn on the show
to discuss a classic investment book.
Ryan Bunn is a curious investor living in Denver, Colorado, where he is the lead portfolio
manager for reference equities, global and international small cap strategies.
Ryan has over 15 years of investment experience across both the public and private markets,
and for this episode, he has selected the Art of Speculation, written by the legendary
investor, Philip Carey.
The Art of Speculation was first published in 1927, and we're thrilled to discuss it on
the show today.
Here comes our conversation with Ryan Bunn.
Hi Ryan and welcome to Investing by the Books podcast.
Hi Eddie, thank you very much for having me today.
It's great to have you on.
Where are we reaching you today?
I am in my office in Denver, Colorado.
Great, and to begin, for those not familiar with you, how did your passion for investing
begin?
Yeah, my interest began at a young age.
My mother introduced me to saving and investing.
I had a few shares of a mutual fund in elementary school, and I'm old enough that we would
look up the prices in the newspaper, but I'm also young enough that I kind of grew up
during the tech bubble, and so over time that transition to an Ameritrade account and everything
moved online.
I've been investing for a long time, but really, I'd say I have a passion for strategy and
business models as well, growing up, I always had some sort of side business going on.
I distributed candy, got in trouble for that middle school, I had some eBay businesses
in high school, and so even today, my passion is kind of, I love talking to magic teams,
learning about their businesses, the business model, the strategy, and it's a joy to do
that professionally.
And how was your path to become a professional investor?
Yeah, so I did not know you could become a professional investor until after college, so I was
a bit sheltered that way, but I started as a consultant out of undergrad and basically
did market research and due diligence for large private equity firms.
So that was my introduction to seeing the buy side, I guess, and I immediately kind of
fell in love with that, doing that research.
And after consulting, I spent the next six years doing direct deals in private equity.
So I've been trained as a private equity investor, again, thinking about the whole business,
buying the whole business.
And so that was really where my foundation was laid.
For the past 10 years, I've been investing in global small caps, taking that same approach
into the public markets.
And you're also a rocious reader, I've understood, you have a stack bookshelf in behind
you.
Yes, that is true.
I don't know when this started, but maybe five or six years ago, I started purchasing
used books, you know, just from the bibliographies of the books I read.
And any time someone referenced the book, that was interesting, you know, I realized you
can usually get them for five or 10 bucks.
So I started buying.
And then when you're surrounded by books, it's hard not to pick them up and read them.
You know, so that is kind of compounded over time.
And how many books do you have now approximately?
Oh, yeah, I don't even know how to guess it, maybe, I don't know, 500 or 1,000, these
are the good ones.
And my basement's kind of overflowing with other ones, but, you know, one of my favorite
authors is Naseem to leave.
And I think he, you know, he's talked about a library of 30,000 books, you know, in libraries
that you won't even read half of the books you own.
So I'm nowhere near that.
So you have many books, and today you have selected one, I guess it was not that easy, but
the one we will speak about is the Art of Speculation.
Can you briefly tell us about what the book is about and structure?
Yeah, and so the Art of Speculation, it's almost a hundred years old, and it was written
by Philip Carey, who was a mutual fund investor, and it's basically his just reflections on
the market.
There's a lot of how-to, he goes through how the, you know, exchanges actually work, how
you buy a stock, how you short sell.
But he also towards the end of the book gets really deeply into, you know, some investment
philosophy, and you know, that was where I really got interested, and I think it's actually
a seminal work in investment philosophy, and I think most philosophies that are in practice
today, you can actually trace back to some of Carey's teachings.
And the title sounds quite promotional and short term to me at least, the Art of Speculation.
Why do you think it's worth reading?
Yeah, there are a number of reasons.
You know, first, I love reading old, you know, financial history books, just for the
reminder about how things very rarely change, you know, so Carey, you know, even to your
point on the title, the Art of Speculation, you know, a hundred years ago, investing in
equities was viewed almost as gambling.
It was a scary proposition, people really focused on the risk, and even through the book,
you know, Carey talks about the psychological aspect of equity investing, of market swings,
and you know, so you find that headlines today for the markets, you know, they're the
same as existed a hundred years ago, and I think that grounding is very important, and
it's always great to get that kind of directly from people at the time who experienced it.
And the author of the book was, as you mentioned, Phil Carey, can you tell us about him?
Who was he?
Yes, and so, you know, the way I came across this book was actually Warren Buffett referenced
Carey.
So, Carey, he was born in 1896, but he lived a long and very fruitful life, and I believe
he attended one of the Berkshire Hathaway annual meetings in the mid-90s, and Buffett,
you know, mentioned his track record, mentioned, you know, how great an investor Carey was,
and so I think that's what led this book to ending up on my bookshelf.
Carey himself had a pretty interesting life, I believe he was a pilot in World War I,
and then began working as a bond salesman for what became paintwebber.
But ultimately, in the mid-1920s, he started one of the first mutual funds in the country.
It was called the Pioneer Fund.
He ended up running that for 50 or 60 years, and developing this incredible track record
of 12 to 13% compounding over that, you know, very lengthy period of time.
So, you know, just based on that track record loan, I was interested to hear what he
had to say about the markets.
And how many books did he write?
Yes, so I believe this was his second book.
So his first book was called Buying a Bond.
I think Warren Buffett actually read that, and it may have led him to actually meet with
Carey before he even started Graham Newman, so Buffett was aware of what Carey was doing
for a very long time.
And I think Cray also has an autobiography that was put together kind of later in his
life.
So, I think I have that on order on the bookshelf somewhere that I'll need to pull out
someday.
And I think his first book was published in 1924.
Yes, that's right, and then he followed up with the Art of Speculation in 27, you know,
so much of it was written before the Depression, you know, but even though the market hadn't
crashed, you know, he was still keenly aware that he was speculating in the equities he
owed.
And there was also a revised edition of the book, right?
Yes, so the edition I have, which you can buy today, is from 1930.
So there were a few updates.
I'm not exactly sure how much change from the 1927 version.
You would have had a few months to get this out and think about, you know, the Great Depression
wanted to see if you wanted to change any of his viewpoints.
It's quite spectacular to read the book and see how well ahead he was.
I mean, you mentioned that he has been very influential and you can see later works that
has been some of the most red books in investing literature.
Can you mention some of those that he inspired?
Yeah, you know, obviously he had an influence on Warren Buffett, you know, there's a lot
of what he says that I actually see reflected in the writings of Philip Fisher, you know,
who's commonly, you know, kind of viewed it as a key Buffett influence as well.
You know, Fisher, I think, has viewed more as a growth investor.
Korea, I believe, would have been more kind of on the value side.
He was not deep in technology or things like that.
But they both had a very similar, you know, way they approached fundamental investing.
And I think that's, you know, where the roots lead back to in a lot of crazy teachings.
It's interesting to see that he's using words and sentences like the intelligent investor,
these kind of terms in the book.
So definitely one step ahead.
But if we go into the insights from the art of speculation, what is the most important
that you have learned?
Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, kind of connecting it to the investment philosophies that
we see today, you know, Korea, one of the quotes that stood out to me was, you know,
he talked about, you know, a non-overstock is favored by the law of compound interest.
And so, you know, today, you hear the word compounder all the time.
You know, I've got at least three books, you know, that have compounder in the title on
the bookshelf.
And so, you know, when I saw that Korea, you know, he had this insight of retained
earnings reinvested, will compound value for that equity shareholder.
And at the time, you know, in 1927, this was, you know, fairly groundbreaking.
People were not discussing stocks in this way.
Equities reviewed his dangerous bonds, valued on dividend yield.
You know, so I thought that was very cool to see.
And he even goes, you know, he kind of provides an even broader framework on fundamental
investing.
There's a section called Men Materials and Money.
And Korea, basically, he starts from first principles.
And literally says, you know, what is a business?
What am I owning when I own stock?
And what, you know, drives that business to create value?
And he comes up with those three points.
And, you know, today, most fundamental investors, their investment philosophy, they want
strong management teams, you know, which, in craze time, we've been the men.
They want a competitive moat.
And to create that was materials.
So what materials and assets to the business zone that, you know, created competitive differentiation.
And then finally money.
And you know, Krayden talked specifically about valuation.
When he talked about, you know, the money in the business, it was the capital.
And so, you know, that encompasses valuation, but also the balance, each strength, the
liquidity the business has, you know, which are all kind of risk metrics that get pushed
aside sometimes.
But he was really looking from first principles on how do I buy great businesses?
And coming back again to the speculation, I mean, he writes a lot about this aspect of
investing.
What does he really mean with that?
Yeah, I mean, you know, again, back a hundred years ago, you know, equities were fairly
new, you know, and Kray, he's a, he's old, he has a lot of history, I guess.
So in the book, you know, he was born in the late 1800s, but he worked with people who
were investing after the Civil War.
So he's actually looking back, referencing the investments that were available to people
between the Civil War and the Spanish-American War.
And so at the time, you know, I think you could have owned some railroad stocks.
And that was nearly it.
And you know, Kray, starting in the 1900s, you know, industrial stocks, businesses that
were not railroads, were new to the markets, and were viewed as very exciting.
And to Kray and most investors at five, you know, that was even speculation because, you
know, it wasn't a stable, a cash flow stream as railroads.
So, you know, to him, I think nearly everything was speculation.
And I also think that there's a very important lesson there.
I spend most of my time looking at small-cap companies.
And in reality, you know, today in the public equity markets, there is a lot of speculation
and gambling going on.
You know, there are a lot of listed businesses that will not be around in five to ten years.
It's, I think it gets lost sometimes when you look at the S&P 500 and you look at indexes
the average it together, you know, how risky parts of the market are.
And Kray knew that.
He's got a chapter specifically on Wildcat Miners, I believe, and back in, before the pressure
that you would just take out a newspaper ad to say you were prospecting for gold and
you could raise money that way.
And most of them were frauds to the point where, you know, I think it was even referenced
that someone found gold and then they wrote, they wrote back to New York and told the
bank, hey, you have to cancel this listing.
We did find gold.
So, it's not a fraud anymore.
Now we're not selling the shares.
So, you know, it was a very speculative time in Kray, you know, he knew that and I think
that led to the title.
Yeah.
And it's, he even writes that it is quite impossible to draw a sharp line and say, of those on
the one side, these are investors and those, the other, they are speculators.
It's an, in fact, speculation is inseparable from investment.
So I guess that's what I really take away from this book that you need to take some risk
and there is some speculation involved, but you can do it more or less risky.
Right.
And that's, you know, I think the last chapter, you know, I think he called it when speculation
becomes investing and that's, you know, it's where he's got all of his kind of insights
wrapped up to tell you, you know, how do you go from gambling to truly being a prudent
investor?
Yes.
And he has the 12 commandments for speculation.
I mean, we can't go through all of them, but if you would have to choose up to three of
them, which are the most important in your view.
Yeah.
Sure.
So, you know, he, the 12 commandments, the amazing thing is I think they are all still
true today, you know, which I give credit for that nearly a hundred years ago.
You know, I think his, his first commandment is to never hold fewer than 10 stocks in five
industries.
And so, you know, this is a very early look at diversification.
And I think this is interesting for a couple of reasons, you know, first, you know, Karei,
you know, he didn't need academic research, you know, and a mathematical definition of
risk to understand the value of diversification, you know, he wrote about a hundred years
ago.
On the other hand, you know, a 10 stock portfolio, you know, today we would not view as
particularly diversified.
So, I think he also understood, you know, the, the ability to outperform markets requires
some level of concentration.
And if you have 60, 80, 100 stocks, you become the index.
So, you know, I think in his first principle, as he's talking about becoming, you know,
an investor on your own, he's, he's describing the way that you have to construct your portfolio
to even have a chance at generating alpha.
Any other lessons you would like to bring up from the commandments?
Yeah, the, the second one, and Philip Fisher actually talks about this as well, but Karei
says to consider yield the least important factor in analyzing a stock.
And so, you know, it was a little bit different in his time in 1930, investors would basically
compare the dividend yield on a stock to a bond they could buy.
That was the way that the valuation was done.
So, you know, obviously his insight was that there's more value to a stock than, than
just a dividend yield.
And, you know, on the one hand, today, that this seems very obvious, nobody, nobody
invests, you know, I don't think based simply on dividend yields today, but at the same
time, today, you know, investors get very excited about buybacks, which are synthetic
dividends.
And so, you know, I think, I see a lot of investment pitches where people are so excited
that there's a lot of cash and the company is now finally going to buyback a bunch of stock.
And in reality, you're kind of adding that buyback yield to the dividend yield and getting
excited about the return you're going to earn.
But implicit in that is that this company has nowhere to reinvest this capital.
And so, you know, I think Karei is getting at that as well when he's talking about ignoring
the yield, it's because he was looking for businesses that were going to redeploy this
capital very productively inside their business.
And so, you know, I find even today, you know, this lesson, I don't think has been internalized
by the market.
And so, you know, I thought that was very cool to see him kind of thinking that way.
I would definitely agree with that.
And there's also a lot of private investors, definitely, who are looking for just high
yield.
That's the only thing they're basing their decisions on.
And there's books on how to find the best yielding stocks and how to prioritize.
And so on.
But it's actually about getting that return on your capital and compounding it and reinvesting.
You know, and in Karei's head, right, he's speculating in equities.
So, you know, if you just look at the yield, you might as well take the extraordinarily low
risk of a bot.
You know, don't be a speculator if you want that yield.
And if you're like getting a slight premium on the yield, I don't know if the risk
would is necessarily worth it.
And if you would choose the third one out of the 12 commandments, which would that be?
Yeah.
The last one, I'd say, he says, seek facts diligently and advice never.
And so, you know, he's basically saying, do your own work.
I think this is another, you know, investment, you know, piece of advice that we view as
kind of trite today.
But it's never lost its relevance.
You know, I think maybe it's done differently today.
It used to be, you know, people hanging around Wall Street and whispering to each other,
I guess, you know, going going into the Great Depression.
But today, I mean, there are obviously platforms where you can follow people as exact portfolios.
And, you know, on the one hand, this transparency is amazing in the industry.
It's great to be able to have people put their money where their mouth is, you know, and
kind of show how the research is doing.
But to me, the reason you have to do your own work, you know, comes back to the conviction
you have in the stock.
So, you know, for Kare to build his track record over, you know, 60 years, he was incredibly
patient.
And I'm sure, to outperform, he would hold stocks through very nasty drawdowns.
And the only way you can do that is when you personally, you know, know the business and
have the conviction, when the market is telling you there's something terribly wrong with
this business to hold on.
And, you know, I think we're all familiar with Amazon after the tech bubble, you know,
trading down 95% or $5 a share.
You know, somebody sold that share at $5.
And my guess is it was not a person who'd met Jeff Bezos and understood the business model.
I guess it was someone who's, you know, friend or uncle told him three years before they
should buy Amazon and they watched it drop 95%.
And so, you know, I think this is something that you see with all great investors, you
are encouraging you to do your own research, to your own work.
And I don't think it's necessarily, you know, that you can't find great ideas.
As other people mentioned, it really comes down to how do you hold that stock for the long
term.
And when I looked at the 1927 edition, the first one, I saw there that there were actually
just 10 commandments.
And then he extended it to 12 in the revised edition.
So one of them was to do your own work.
The one you mentioned was already in the first one, but he added another one, which was
to avoid inside information as you would the plague.
And then he added be flexible, ignore mechanical formulas for valuing securities.
Interesting.
Well, to, you know, I guess thinking back to the great depression, right, I mean, this
was a time when insider trading was effectively legal.
You know, so that was definitely a market nuance that is, you know, hopefully different
today.
And yeah, to your point, I'm being flexible on the valuation metrics.
Yeah, the valuation is something I'm sure that that was in his, in his head at all times.
And, you know, I would say, you know, that means that another one of his lessons was to avoid
leverage.
And so he, I mean, he actually had that in the book before leverage hurt a lot of people,
you know, in the great depression.
And yeah, it's interesting.
I think his book has so many lessons and, you know, the wording and verbiage he uses is
different, right?
So he talks about, you know, when he says avoid leverage, he means don't buy on margin.
And I think today, you know, I don't think there are that many investors, you know, hugely
margined in their trading accounts.
But there are many investors that are in, you know, triple levered ETFs.
And many investors using zero day options.
And so, you know, we found a way to embed leverage into these markets in a way that, you know,
isn't described as margin, you know, but, but the lessons still, still is there from
career.
Yeah, and we touched upon it a little bit regarding how relevant his ideas are today.
Maybe there's something else you would like to mention.
Yeah, you know, this is the, this topic, I think, is a little scary to mention, I guess,
as an active investor.
But Karei is a couple chapters where he talks about market cycles.
And so, you know, on the one hand, active investors, you know, especially as we come, you
know, we're in a very extended bull market, I would say today.
And so, you know, talking about market cycles means you've been wrong for at least a decade.
And so it's not a, not a popular thing to discuss, but, you know, Karei, he was aware of
the macro environment, you know, one of his lessons was when, when stocks are very high,
when things are frothy, you know, hold some short-term bonds.
So he was aware of the market cycles, you know, I think when you look at Buffett, you know,
as much as Buffett says, buy and hold, and passive indexes are great, you know, he plays
market cycles.
And he's done it very successfully, and today he's record cash.
And Howard Marx, you know, he writes books about market cycles.
So I think it's amazing that all these great investors with amazing track records, they're
aware of what the market is doing, even if it's tough to talk about, and you don't want
to make predictions on the top or the bottom, they've found a way to profitably navigate
around, you know, the psychological swings that within the market.
It's clear that you are a big fan of Karei and his ideas, but is there anything that
you don't agree with him on?
Yeah, there are a few things that haven't aged perfectly from the book, I guess.
You know, at the time, and in the book, you know, his insight on retained earnings comes
from some analysis he was able to do, looking at stocks that paid dividends versus stocks
that didn't pay dividends.
And that's where he could kind of see the reinvestment begin.
And you know, this was very challenging to do.
You know, people were taking pen and pencil, you know, and trying to calculate, you know,
all these returns, you know, the graphs that show up in these books were hand drawn at
the time.
You know, so when you see a stock chart, you know, from 1990 to 1930, someone was literally
drawing that.
So, you know, I think to him, he was at the early stages of statistical analysis, technical
analysis, and you know, he's got a couple of chapters in the book where I think he's
excited about this and he sees, you know, that maybe there's some insights that come out
of this.
You know, a hundred years later, I think what's more interesting to me is that his fundamental
investing tenets have aged better than finding, you know, some key or some trading mechanism
buried in the charts.
And I imagine, you know, if he had written, you know, another investing book in 1970,
I think he would have dropped some of those chapters.
Yeah, but it's fascinating to read it, I think, to understand how the markets have changed.
I mean, there's just, of course, terminology, but also how you would invest, how accessible
it is, how expensive it is to invest in, there's a lot of lessons in that aspect as well,
I think.
That's very true.
And, you know, he's from a time of ticker tape, right, where, you know, you had no idea
what price the stock was trading at when you bought it, you know, right, like even Warren
Buffett and Omaha, right, you know, you're, I don't know, you know, how many minutes behind
the actual stock market you are, you know, and today we're talking, you know, nanoseconds
or something to get your price good.
So it is a different environment for sure.
Yeah, this kind of tape reading, but if you could meet him today, if he was alive, what would
you ask him?
Yeah, you know, I would love to know about his process.
So that's something he didn't discuss it in the book too much.
It's clear his philosophy, what he looked for in businesses, but, you know, I would love

Did he know the mantra teams he was investing in, you know, how he actually went about analyzing
the businesses that he invested in.
You know, similarly, for any investor with an amazing track, I always love to know how
they think about valuation.
As you mentioned, one of his rules was, you know, there's no, you know, mechanical specific
valuation formula to rely on.
It is more art than science and valuation, and so, you know, Buffett has, he's talked
about this a lot as well, but it's always valuable, I think, to hear how great investors
truly know when to pull the trigger on an investment.
Have you read his autobiography?
Not yet, but I'm very excited too, and, you know, I'm hoping that maybe, when he talks
a bit more about himself, maybe he'll tell a bit more about, you know, what he was doing.
Yeah, and I think, you know, not the Brent Buffett too much, but going back to Buffett again,
you know, I think they're increasingly great stories to hear about Buffett with the
crazy diligence he was doing, you know, when, when he was a young investor, which I think
also gets lost, you know, today he can sit in Omaha and, you know, I think it's different.
But he was on the ground, pounding pavement, you know, showing up at Geico on the weekends,
chatting with people.
I imagine Karei would have very similar stories that would be very cool, kind of, due diligence
insights.
Hmm, some field work and channel checks, yeah, that would be exciting to read about.
I haven't read the autobiography yet either, but I'm intrigued to do so after this conversation.
But let's shift focus a bit and hear about you as an investor.
You are the founder of Reference Equity, please tell us about the firm.
Yeah, so Reference Equity, we are a small cap focused boutique investment firm.
We're long only, we have two strategies, global small cap and international small cap.
And we're attempting to take, you know, this investment philosophy that described by Karei
and others and apply it into the, you know, what we view are inefficient small cap markets.
We have fairly concentrated portfolios and ultimately, you know, our clients view us as
